mercy_translation.text:
We must anticipate in our defense things that others might say. Someone may perhaps argue: if his death had to occur in the sight of all and with witnesses so that the message of the resurrection might be believed, he should at least have devised for himself a glorious death, merely avoiding the disgrace of the cross.

But if he had done this, he would have given grounds for suspicion against himself, as though he had power not over every kind of death but only over the one he had devised for himself. Then there would again have been no less an excuse for unbelief concerning the resurrection. Therefore the death of the body came not from himself but from hostile plotting, so that whatever death they brought upon the Savior, he might destroy that very death.

It is like a noble wrestler, great in skill and courage, who does not choose his own opponents lest he give reason to suspect cowardice toward some. Rather, he gives the choice to the spectators, especially if they happen to be enemies, so that whichever opponent they set against him he may throw down and be believed superior to all.

So too the Life of all, our Lord and Savior Christ, did not devise a death for his own body lest he appear to fear another. Rather, he accepted and endured on the cross the death given by others—and especially by enemies—the death they considered terrible, dishonorable, and to be avoided. Thus when this death too was destroyed, he himself might be believed to be Life and the power of death might be completely abolished.

A marvelous and paradoxical thing has therefore happened: the death they thought dishonorable to inflict became the trophy over death itself. For this reason he did not undergo the death of John by beheading, nor was he sawn apart like Isaiah, so that even in death he might preserve the body undivided and whole, and no excuse might be given to those who wished to divide the Church.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
The wrestler analogy explains why Christ does not choose a supposedly easier or more honorable death.
The closing ecclesial application links the undivided body of Christ with the unity of the Church.
